subject: swampTroll
pitch:
Category: Monster.
Subject: swamp troll with tusks, mohawk and bone fetishes.
Style: Blizzard/Warcraft.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for building a Warcraft-style swamp troll, thinking through the SDK imports and structure needed to keep the generation robust without being able to test it directly.

I'm sketching the troll's design: a hunched, ~2.2m tall creature with heavy shoulders, long arms, digitigrade legs, and big feet, done in teal-green skin with a crimson mohawk, ivory tusks, bone fetishes, and a swamp-themed base with moss, mushrooms, and lily pads. I'm now working out the skeleton proportions, placing hips, spine, chest, neck, and head positions to capture the hunched posture.

Setting up the neck chain's parent to the last spine joint, then adding a head joint attached to the neck tip with its own orientation.

For the jaw, I'm thinking through how to position it relative to the head using local offsets, and considering defining a helper function for consistent head-relative coordinates rather than hardcoding absolute positions each time.

Since I'm not rotating the head joint, I decide absolute model-space positions are simpler and avoid axis confusion. I'm now sketching the troll-like head design: heavy brow, hooked nose, tusked jaw, swept-back pointed ears, deep-set eyes, built from a scaled skull sphere centered around a fixed head point.

I'm planning the facial geometry — a brow ridge box, a curved hooked nose tube, a separate frustum-shaped muzzle, and a heavier lower jaw box attached to the jaw joint with upward tusks and a dark mouth interior between the jaws. For eyes, I'm considering small glowing yellow spheres with dark pupils, possibly using a darker eye socket shape to simplify the pupil effect.

Positioning the eye plane slightly outward on the skull sphere surface so the brow ridge partially covers it, then working out angled brow rods on each side slanting toward center for an angry look.

That flat disc looks like a plate floating above the surface, so I'm switching to a small embedded sphere eyeball instead, protruding slightly from the socket with a glowing amber color and a dark flattened pupil sphere positioned toward the front.

Now I'm designing the ears—skipping sunken eye rings since the brow handles that, and moving to long troll ears that sweep back and up, planning them as a flat extruded outline shape lying in the frontal plane with a sweeping, pointed curve.

I'm checking that the ear's polygon outline doesn't self-intersect, tracing through each edge's slope to confirm the sharp tip and back curve stay clean.

Now I'm sizing and positioning the ear relative to the head, choosing a scale and offset, and working out orthogonal x/y direction vectors so the extrusion sweeps back correctly without distorting the shape.

Next I'm planning the mohawk as a signature feature: a ridge of overlapping blade shapes running from forehead to nape, each tall and tapering with a root-to-tip color gradient, assembling roughly nine blades along the skull's centerline.

Still refining blade geometry...

Working through the extrusion direction and cross product to confirm thickness lies along the X axis, then considering adding flanking smaller blades offset in x for fullness.

Now I'm picking the color palette: teal-green skin with a paler belly, contrasted against a vivid mohawk gradient from deep crimson/violet root to a hot orange-pink tip for visual pop.

I'm also layering in voodoo accessories—ivory bone fetishes, a brown loincloth with purple accents, wood-and-bone bracers, feathers, and a glowing green totem staff topped with a skull with eerie eyes. I need to keep the staff shorter than the troll itself (around 1.9m) so the subject remains the tallest element in the scene.

Now I'm working out the arm pose: the right arm hangs loosely with a closed fist, while the left arm grips the staff planted beside the body, using bent-elbow inverse kinematics to connect shoulder and hand positions realistically.

Rethinking the rest pose itself — rather than gripping the staff tightly, I'll keep both arms hanging loosely out from the body with fingers spread, satisfying the "separated and extended limbs" requirement while letting the staff stand as a nearby prop instead of forcing a grip.

I'll move the staff into a larger totem pole set behind the troll, adorned with skulls and feathers, scaled shorter than the troll so the figure stays the visual focus. I'm also adding bone and skull fetish details like a necklace to tie the troll and totem together thematically.

Now I'm shaping the body itself, planning a sweep or loft along a spine path to get the hunched, lanky swamp-troll torso with wide shoulders and a narrow waist, using a chain of bones through the hips and spine to drive the cross-section.

Now I'm thinking through the skin paint, using countershading with mottled texture blending two greenish tones for a darker belly and lighter top, then adding scattered wart spots for texture.

For the feet, I'm planning a custom paint function that mixes the base skin color with mud based on height, using a smoothstep and noise to fade the mud effect near the ground.

Now I'm thinking about adding a Warcraft-style aesthetic with bold proportions and painterly flat colors, plus tribal war paint decals—stripes on the face and a voodoo glyph on the chest—applied using a decal function that overlays textures onto specific body parts like the skull.

For the chest decal, I need to figure out where on the torso's surface the glyph should sit, casting a ray forward from a point near the chest to find the correct hit location, then guarding against a null result if the ray misses the surface.

Now I'm working out the legs — giving these trolls short, sturdy limbs with hips, forward-bent knees, and big flat feet, calculating the joint positions and segment lengths needed for the two-part leg structure.

For the foot, I'm scaling a sphere to form a flattened pad attached at the ankle tip joint, then adding three clawed toe shapes pointing forward. I need to position the pad's center carefully so its bottom edge sits right at y=0, keeping the foot flush with the ground.

Setting ankle y and foot offset, then tapering the shin and adding a knobby knee sphere. Going with three toes per foot for the troll look. Now placing shoulder joints slightly inset from the torso with pauldron spheres, and starting the arm chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints.

For hands, I'm planning four fingers plus a thumb per hand, each finger as a short two-joint chain with a claw spike at the tip, parented to the wrist joint, keeping fingers extended in the rest pose.

Now I'm sketching a hand-building function that places the palm along the wrist's pointing direction and spaces fingers across it with a slight spread, generating the chain points for each finger so they sweep outward realistically.

For the thumb, I'm angling its direction inward toward the body rather than straight down, mirroring this for left and right arms, and considering whether to keep both hanging hands fully symmetrical or vary one arm's pose slightly for a more natural stance.

Trolls have no tail, so I'll skip that and instead focus on adding a hunched back with a hump and some ridge-like spine bumps along the upper torso to suggest a rugged, bony silhouette.

Actually, since the mohawk blades already run down the back, I'll let those continue toward the mid-back instead of adding separate spikes. For the torso, I'm planning a leather belt with a skull buckle and dangling bone fetishes, plus a loincloth with front and back flaps carrying a painted pattern.

For the loincloth texture, I'm thinking through using double-sided textured cards rather than extrude, since extrude only takes flat color. I'll place a hip-front card at the attachment point facing up with a lean of 180 degrees so it drapes straight down, sized around .32 by .4, textured with an SVG zigzag-trimmed cloth pattern featuring a skull emblem.

Now I'm working out the spine path coordinates for the torso and where the belt line sits at hip height, tracing the surface geometry to find where the loincloth should attach along the front of the pelvis.

I'm refining the loop placement near the hip's spine joint, worried the cut at the tube cap is too close to the equator, so I'm specifying an explicit point and direction slightly higher up to make the belt cut cleaner before sweeping it into a belt mesh.

Settling on a boxy section with a small radius so the belt reads as a flat leather strap rather than a round rope, then moving on to positioning a skull-shaped buckle at the front.

For the skull, I'm raycasting against the torso surface to find a front-facing attachment point, then sketching out a `skull` helper built from a sphere cranium, a box jaw, dark eye sockets, and a nose hole, oriented using an aim/quaternion function so it faces outward correctly.

Adding eye sockets and nose holes to each skull, totaling around 40 low-poly parts across 8 skulls, and setting up the `aim` helper to orient parts along a direction vector with a fallback for parallel cases. Now I'm planning the necklace of bones and fangs as a closed loop draped around the neck, computing ellipse points to feed into a catmull-rom curve.

Rather than using a ring primitive, I'm manually drawing a closed path of points around the neck and chest, then draping that path onto the torso surface so each sample point snaps to the nearest surface location for a natural fit.

Now I'm figuring out how to place hanging beads like fangs and skulls along that cord — I want each bead oriented to hang downward rather than following the path's tangent, so I'm checking how the along/ring callbacks expose frame and position data to attach parts correctly.

For the fang geometry, I'm using a small cone shape and thinking through how to offset and translate it so the base sits at the attachment point while the tip points straight down.

Now I'm planning the alternating bead pattern along the necklace—fangs, small sphere beads, and bone cylinder segments—plus a central skull fetish as the main pendant, and considering a dangling belt fetish made of crossed bones, feathers, and cord.

For the hanging fetishes I'm designing a bone rod with knobbed ends, a crossbar bone, a tiny skull, a feather, and a cord-wrap torus, hung three per side from the hip bone. I'm also working out wrist cuffs as lathed rings following the forearm's profile.

Placing the cuff 75% down the forearm, between elbow and wrist, lathed around that axis using the elbow joint as the bone reference since it carries the forearm segment. I'm also considering adding a shoulder embellishment, maybe a curved horn or tusk shape for one pauldron, keeping both shoulders symmetrical with some spiked detail.

Working out the shoulder pads now: a simple lathed dome with bone spikes on both sides, maybe varying material slightly between a hide-textured pad and a bone-studded one with feather accents, but keeping the overall silhouette consistent since bone fetishes are the main focus. For the head, I'm sketching out tusk geometry curving from the lower jaw outward and upward past the upper lip using a bezier sweep, sizing them fairly large and working out the relative coordinates from the head center.

Now I'm defining the exact tusk curve with start, control, and end points so it rises up near the nose level, giving it a tapering ivory-colored radius with grain texture and anchoring it to the jaw bone. I'm also adding smaller upper fangs and a decorative ring or torus band at the tusk base, working out how to orient that torus using the tangent of the bezier path so it wraps correctly around the curve.

Next I'm sizing that ring against the tusk's radius at that point, then shifting to building the lower jaw as a tapered box shape running from the hinge to the chin, adding a rounded chin piece, and considering whether to add a small row of teeth along the jaw before deciding to skip it for now.

Now I'm adding dark cone teeth and a dark red mouth interior box between the jaws, plus positioning the jaw hinge joint and its aim direction. I'm also building the upper jaw/muzzle as a tapered box, then sculpting a large hooked nose using a bezier sweep with tapering radius, adding dark nostril spheres, and reusing the skin color/paint scheme while considering how dense the painting needs to be.

Now I'm placing cheekbone spheres and heavy brow-ridge rods on the skull, then scattering warts as small sphere clusters across both the skull and torso for extra texture. I'm thinking through Warcraft-style proportions with wide shoulders and bulky pauldrons, then planning the swamp base scene with a circular mud platform, moss, a glossy water puddle, lily pads, reeds, glowing mushrooms, skulls and stones, a totem placed behind-left, and a bubbling green cauldron.

I'm working out the cauldron placement behind-right so the front stays clear, and figuring out the base geometry so the troll's feet sit correctly on the platform surface—making sure the lowest points touch floor level within the allowed 2% tolerance by carefully offsetting the base height and troll position together.

Actually, if I offset just the root joint's position, that could shift the whole hierarchy including the base — instead I should build the base with its bottom sunk slightly below y=0, so the base itself handles the "sinking into mud" effect without needing a global offset.

Translating only the root might be okay since joints above are unscaled, but it's risky with the floor constraint that nothing should hang below the ground. A cleaner fix is to bake a constant Y offset directly into the helper function where each part gets defined, rather than shifting the root after the fact.

I'll set the base top at F = 0.05 and have the troll's feet sit exactly there, then define all other coordinates (hips, spine, neck, head, limbs) as that offset plus their relative height so everything stays consistent.

That actually works nicely — the troll's feet sink slightly into the mud with no awkward offset needed. I'll make the base a lathe shape with a gentle raised rim/mound profile, topping out around 0.06, so the toes sit partially buried right at that mud surface.

I'm raising the toe rod to y=.07 so it's visible above the mud line, then thinking through the base paint: mottled dark brown and green mud tones with moss patches using noise, plus a thin murky teal-green puddle disc near the front with ripple and lily-pad details. Now I'm sketching out the texture list, starting with decorative war-paint elements since the eyes are handled by spheres already.

I'm planning the remaining textures: face paint, chest glyph decal, loincloth cloth cards, feather cards for mohawk/totem/fetish, reed and lily textures, and a carved totem-face design painted onto the stacked totem pole segments using decals. I'm also considering mushroom spots, glowing orb details, and a glowing rune ring laid flat around the troll's feet using a circle geometry with voodoo glyphs.

Now I'm working out placement details for that rune ring so it glows green and sits just above the base without clipping, plus adding glow to totem eyes and the cauldron brew. I'm steering clear of SVG text rendering in favor of paths, and settling on a swamp green-teal color palette for the troll's skin with amber eyes, ivory tusks, and contrasting orange-red mohawk and rust/purple loincloth for visual pop.

Setting up shared skin paint and imports...

Adding mud blending near the base...

Still writing paint logic...

Setting up the skeleton structure now with a random generator and hip joint as the root, deciding whether to assign spine roles explicitly since the pelvis naturally serves as the first spine joint. Starting to build the spine chain with a catmull curve through joint positions.

Adding neck and head joints...

Head top around 1.92, mohawk extending to 2.15, giving a total height near 2.1-2.2, consistent with a troll's real scale, so totem height should stay at 1.9 or below. I'm placing the jaw joint just below and in front of the head center, aimed forward-down so the jaw bone reads naturally. Now I'm setting up the torso sweep with a radius function driving its taper along the spine.

Defining a piecewise linear ramp function for the torso's radius keyframes, plus a generic curve helper, with rounded sweep caps blending into the neck tube. I'm skipping a pot belly, adding a hump sphere at the upper back scaled for a hunched look, and tapering the neck sweep radius to connect cleanly into the head.

Now I'm shaping the shoulders with trapezius lumps and adding a skull sphere parented to the head bone, deciding whether to use smooth shading or faceted flat-shaded accents to match a stylized Warcraft-like look rather than fully painterly.

I'm sketching a helper function to generate reusable sphere "blob" shapes with position, color, bone, and scale parameters, and defining a typed 3-number vector alias to keep positions consistent, planning out the first head part as a skull blob attached at the head bone.

Now I'm adding the back-skull lump for the sloping troll forehead, then working out brow ridge rods using a mirrored sign convention for left/right placement, and starting dark eye socket blobs positioned relative to the head coordinates.

Rather than a separate socket, I'll simplify by placing the eyeball directly under the brow with a cheek beneath it, then add a subtle darker upper-lid blob slightly offset above and in front of the eye to suggest shading.

I'm checking the eyeball placement against the skull surface curvature — the eyeball protrudes only slightly past the surface, giving it a nicely buried, socketed look with the pupil facing forward. Next I'm placing a cheek blob below and outward from the eye, then building the muzzle as a tapered box frustum running forward from the face.

Now I'm shaping the nose and nostrils using a bezier sweep for the nose bridge and small dark blobs for the nostril openings, then adding small ivory fang spikes jutting down from the muzzle.

Working out the lower jaw placement, I'm checking that its top surface sits below the muzzle's bottom edge so there's a proper mouth gap rather than overlapping geometry, adjusting the jaw's vertical center accordingly relative to the skull's base.

Positioning the tusks with a curved path from the jaw base outward and upward...

Still working out tusk shape and texture...

Now for the ears, then a small braided chin tendril detail in red for extra character, plus bone/tusk ear ornaments and a feather accent. I'm also planning a decal-based war paint pattern across the skull's eyes using an SVG overlay.

I'll target the decal surface to the skull and cheek blobs together, letting the projection ray pick the nearest hit, and keep the lift minimal so it sits just under the eyeballs. Now I'm sketching the actual face paint as an SVG design.

Now I'm working out the mohawk geometry, computing station coordinates along the skull curve by solving for where the forehead surface intersects each height.

For the lower stations I need to ray-cast onto the neck and torso surfaces instead, sweeping z from 0.36 down to 0.06 to find where the hump and neck tops meet the skull base, then sort all the hit points together and orient each blade vertically, tilting slightly backward to follow the surface normal.

Varying blade height along the mohawk path—tall at the forehead and crown, tapering down the nape and back—and assigning each blade to the nearest bone joint (head, neck, or spine) so it deforms correctly, then extruding each blade with a tapered thickness and the mohawk color.

Defining blade outline shape...

Checking that DE stays above CD confirms no edge crossing, so the shape is convex enough and fine as a tip, with k scaled to a minimum of .5.

I'll color the blades using the mohawk paint gradient, normalizing by the outline's max height (~.3) to get a paint factor, noting the base dips negative. I'll mark only the tip D as "sharp" with zero smoothing, and plan to add a few feather cards hanging from the back of the head near the ear.

For additional fetish detail I'm adding twin braided dreadlocks at the nape with bone beads — three per side, built as bezier tubes tapering in radius, colored dark red, each dread carrying a couple of bone bead blobs placed along its path. I'm also sketching a chest glyph decal for torso adornment, then moving on to defining shoulder and relaxed hanging hand positions for the arms.

I'm checking that the shoulder-to-hand distances and segment lengths work out to a nearly straight arm with just a slight bend, so the troll's long limbs reach down near knee height while staying well separated from the thighs. I'm figuring out the elbow bend direction for the inner joint and setting up the proper bends parameter format before building the arm chain.

Now I'm defining the arm chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints parented to the spine, then tapering the radius along the arm from shoulder to wrist for a natural limb shape.

Adding muscle blobs for bicep and forearm, then starting on the hand function that computes wrist direction to orient the palm and fingers.

Placing finger bases along the lateral axis with slight spread and curl, computing each segment's joints by extending along a curved direction vector for a natural bent-finger pose.

Positioning the thumb base so it angles down-inward-forward, giving ten chains total across both hands (5 fingers × 2), each with its own sweep and claw. I'm thickening finger radii for a chunkier, Warcraft-style hand, and settling on a dull yellowish-bone tone for the claws rather than ivory or dark bone.

Now I'm working out leg geometry: hip, knee, and ankle positions with limb lengths set so the leg bends forward slightly outward, then defining the chain names and parent relationship for the hip joint. I'm shaping the thigh as a thick muscular sweep, adding a knee blob, and building the foot pad plus three toe rods with small claw spikes at each tip.

For the ankle joint, I'm deciding to grab it directly as the last joint in the leg's joint array rather than relying on a possibly-null tip reference, to keep the typing safe. Now I'm moving on to the loincloth, setting up a belt loop around the hips and casting a ray from the torso surface to find the attachment point for the front hanging card frame.

I'm working out that the frame orientation should face upward, using the plain hit point so it binds to the nearest joint like the spine or hips, then building the card itself with a double-sided cloth texture sized and leaned to hang vertically—though I'm wary the thighs might poke through it.

For clearance, the front cloth sits a bit ahead of the thigh surface so it stays clear, and I'm tilting the lean angle slightly off straight-down (around 160 degrees) so the cloth flares forward naturally with the flow direction instead of hanging perfectly flat. Now I need to set up the matching back flap using a ray cast from behind the torso.

I'm sketching out the decorative texture plan: the cloth gets a rust-red field with a dark banded top of bone-yellow triangles, a central emblem, and a zigzag fringe cut into the bottom edge; feathers get their own vane-shaped texture with a center line for use on the mohawk and totem decorations; and the totem itself is built as a stacked pole of carved head segments.

For the totem specifically, I'm using box geometries where each face shows a different carved design -- a troll face, a bird beak, a skull -- stacked as three segments on a textured wooden pole, topped by a larger glowing-eyed skull with feathers for the crown.

I'm adding a horizontal crossbone lashed through the pole with hanging bone fetishes and feathers for detail, while keeping the totem's overall height capped below the troll's mohawk so it stays the tallest element. I'm placing the totem off to the side with a slight rotation so its carved faces angle toward the troll figure.

Now I'm shaping the cauldron: a lathed iron pot profile forming a solid shell closed at the top with a separate glowing green brew disc sitting just above the rim to suggest bubbling liquid.

Finalizing proportions: pot top flat at .4, brew disc recessed slightly below the rim torus for depth, then adding small cone legs and glowing bubble spheres to complete the piece.

I'm adding a stir stick as a bone across the rim, then clustering reed cards around the back of the cauldron near a totem using angled frame placements with slight bending for a natural reed look. I'm also planning flat lily pad cards on the puddle surface, leaning them to lie nearly flat.

Simplifying the lily pads to upward-facing circle geometry with a notch for the lily texture, then placing a couple of puddles with slightly different coloring at the front-left of the scene, positioned so they stay out of the main composition. Now I'm thinking through glowing mushrooms with domed caps and purple spotted stems for added atmosphere.

I'm scattering a few bones using a rod helper that draws a cylindrical body with knob spheres at each end for a femur-like look, colored with the bone material. Since scenery props lack real joints, I'm thinking through how to attach them to the nearest joint, like the hips, for positioning purposes.

Since there can only be one true root joint, I'm restructuring so a new root joint sits at the origin, with hips as its child, and adding a separate base joint for props parented to root at a slight offset so scenery pieces can attach there without affecting the skeleton's animation chains.

Now I'm writing the skull helper function, which builds a cranium and jaw from spheres and boxes oriented using a quaternion aim direction, scaled and positioned relative to a given anchor point and bone.

I'm checking the eye socket placement against the skull surface curvature, finding they poke out slightly which actually works fine visually, reading as dark bulging sockets.

Now I'm tallying skull counts across the scene—troll pendant, belt buckle, hanging items, totem, ground scatter—totaling around ten skulls at roughly 6 parts each. I'm also sketching out a fetish doll helper hanging piece with a cord, bone cross, tiny skull topper, feather, and red wrap torus.

Next I'm designing feather card attachments and pauldron shoulder armor—a lathed bone dome shape tilted outward with a ring of bone spikes around it, using leather-grained paint for the shoulder piece.

I could instead pass the shoulder joint itself as the frame's position argument, letting it carry its bone automatically, then offset outward from there to compute the pauldron center.

Actually, I'll skip trying to use a ring helper for the spikes and instead place each one manually, computing perpendicular vectors around the shoulder axis to position and orient each spike individually. I'll also set up a bone color palette with light and darker tones for the chest beads and torus shapes.

Now I'm designing a voodoo-style glyph decal for the chest using a red-and-white spiral and triangle motif, then figuring out where to project it onto the torso surface -- working out the spine's tangent direction near the chest so the decal's normal and orientation actually face forward correctly.

Computing the actual tangent gives roughly 28° from vertical, so the belly normal is closer to (0,-0.5,0.87), confirming my decal direction estimate was reasonable. I realize I can just use the hit's normal directly for the decal direction since passing a Hit object automatically sets dir to its normal—simpler than hand-computing it.

For the belt loop placement, I'm checking that the chosen point sits near the spine axis at that height, then working out a perpendicular direction to the spine tangent so the loop wraps the torso correctly rather than slicing along its length.

Now I'm sketching the belt sweep itself — a rope-like leather strap following the loop path with a rounded cross-section, then planning to scatter small stud spheres along it at regular intervals.

For the studs I'll place small gold spheres oriented along the belt path's tangent frames, using a second offset loop with slightly more lift so they sit just above the belt surface. I'm also starting to work out explicit hip positions for hanging fetish items dangling off the belt.

Checking those hip positions against thigh geometry, I realize hanging the fetishes straight down at x=.2 would intersect the thighs, so I need to shift them forward near the loincloth front, roughly at z around .07-.1 offset from the hip center, clear of both the thighs and arms.

I'm checking whether the thighs' x-range actually overlaps the cloth's width, since the knee bends forward enough that its z could poke past the cloth's z. The thighs span roughly x .07 to .35 while the cloth sits around ±.18, so there's clear overlap in x, meaning I need the cloth to stay forward of the thigh fronts in z to avoid clipping.

Some minor clipping is acceptable since a loincloth naturally drapes against the legs, but I'll shift the cloth's attachment point slightly forward and flare it outward a bit more to reduce the intersection. Moving on, I'm now sketching the totem pole geometry using a tapered cylinder shape.

Still writing totem pole code...

Still plotting wing outline points...

For rope bindings I'll add small torus rings around the pole, rotated to lie horizontal. I'm deciding to skip the crossbar and instead add dangling fetishes from the second block.

The totem is coming together with three blocks, trim, wings, skull, horns, feathers, glow eyes, and rope, plus a ring of dark flattened stones at the base. For the glow elements I'm covering amber troll eyes, green skull eyes, runes, brew, mushrooms, wisps, and the pendant fetish. Now I'm designing the runes texture as an SVG with concentric circle outlines and bone-like glyph strokes in green, working out the stroke widths and viewbox scaling, with twelve glyph marks spaced around the ring.

I'm placing alternating triangle and cross-line glyphs rotated around the circle, then adding a dashed inner ring, and working out the geometry so the glyph circle, totem, cauldron, and base don't overlap awkwardly -- adjusting radii and positions so the troll's feet and hands stay comfortably inside the rune ring.

Now I'm shaping the muddy base as a lathed, irregular blob outline extruded with a slight bevel, using a wavy radius function with multiple sine terms to make the rim look uneven and organic rather than a perfect circle.

For coloring, I'm blending a mottled brown mud texture with mossy green patches based on surface normal (more moss on upward-facing areas) and noise, darkening slightly near the rim, while planning to handle any standing water puddles as separate geometry rather than part of the paint shader.

Now I'm working out the vertical placement of the troll's foot so it sinks naturally into the mud: adjusting toe rod heights, foot pad center, and ankle position so the lowest point rests at the base (y=0) while the visible foot sits sunk about 0.045 units into the mud surface at 0.075.

With heights settled, I'm shifting to listing the SVG textures needed: face paint, glyphs, cloth, feathers, runes, reeds, lily, and three totem pole faces—about ten textures total to write out.

For the totem faces, I'm sketching three designs on a dark wood background with border lines: a troll face with tusks and brow, a bird face with a triangular beak and concentric eye circles, and a skull/spirit face with a spiral motif. Writing SVG code...

Still writing SVG coordinates...

Making the skull bone-colored with a dark backdrop and green eyes. I'm checking stroke widths against the viewBox scaling to keep cut-out textures like feathers, reeds, runes, and facepaint readable at render size, then starting on the facepaint stripe pattern with sufficiently thick strokes.

Now I'm working out decal placement and projection direction so the stripe pattern lands correctly on the skull and cheek regions when viewed from the front, accounting for mirrored symmetry.

For the glyph icon, I'm sketching a stylized ceremonial mask motif in deep red tones—concentric circles with a dashed inner ring and a triangular shape overlaying them.

Now I'm shifting to designing the cloth piece as an SVG shape with a zigzag fringe at the bottom and a contrasting top band, using deep burgundy and dark trim colors.

Still writing SVG code...

Moving to the reed icon, I'm sketching a tapered green blade with a thin stem and a brown cattail ellipse near the top, then starting on the lily shape with a notched circular petal outline.

Still working out the arc sweep direction and leaf vein details before moving to the runes circle design.

Writing glyph rune code...

Adding the blob helper...

Confirming Paint is usable as a type import, then defining a Col alias combining string and Paint colors. I'm starting the main build function, setting up a seeded rng and beginning to define the joint hierarchy for the troll's root and base.

Still writing joint chain...

I'm checking that the hip-to-ankle distances match the segment lengths, and confirming the limb function's output feeds correctly into chain with the contact point option set. Then I move to defining the leg sweep radii tapering from thigh to ankle.

Now I'm building the arms as a limb from shoulder to hand with a slight bend, verifying shoulder-to-hand distance stays within the combined segment lengths, and checking that hand position roughly aligns with knee height for a natural dangle.

I'm setting up hand orientation so fingers spread laterally with palms facing inward toward the thighs, then adding a deltoid blob to cover the shoulder with the pauldron. Now I'm starting the torso sweep along the spine with a tapering radius profile from neck to hips, defined through a ramp function.

I need to fix the ramp function's return type since TypeScript might infer a generic number array instead of a fixed tuple, so I'll annotate it explicitly as `[number, number]`. I'm also considering whether to add pec or belly blobs for extra chest definition, but deciding to skip them, and thinking about whether to paint visible ribs to match the lean troll physique.

Now I'm placing an upper back hump blob positioned behind and above the torso's top point to create a hunched silhouette, checking it integrates with the mohawk ray stations along the nape. I'm adding trapezius blobs at the neck base and setting the neck sweep radius so the path from torso to head reads naturally, then placing a deltoid shoulder blob under where the pauldron will sit.

Writing head function...

Combining the torso, hump, and trapezius parts into a single surface so mohawk rays can hit them correctly, and doing the same for the skull plus its back lump to build a head surface. I'm working out the z-coordinate stations for neck and hump rays, checking how the hump's spread in z overlaps the neck tube so the ray hits land correctly.

Now computing the head stations across their z-range, verifying each ray against the skull sphere's geometry including the back lump center, and sorting out which bone (head vs. neck vs. spine) each blade should attach to based on its z position.
